Gravitation and Work Done

Universal Law of Gravitation

  • Newton put forward the universal law of gravitation in 1687 and used it to explain the observed motions of the planets and moons.

#### Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

  • It states that "Every particle attracts every other particle in the universe with force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them".

#### The Universal Gravitation Equation

F ∝ m₁m₂ / r²

F = G m₁m₂ / r²

  • F is the gravitational force between bodies, m₁ and m₂ are the masses of the bodies, r is the distance between the centres of two bodies, G is the universal gravitational constant.
  • The value of G is found to be G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg² (Discovered experimentally by Henry Cavendish in 1798).
  • The gravitational force is both a non-contact force (acting at a distance) and a conservative force (work done is independent of path and work done in a closed path is zero).

Kepler's Planetary Laws (1609)

#### First Law: Law of Orbit

  • It states that "Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun as a focus".

#### Second Law: Law of Area

  • It states that "The line joining the planet and the Sun sweep out equal areas in equal interval of time".

#### Third Law: Law of Time Period

  • It states that "The square of the time period of revolution of a planet around the Sun is directly proportional to the cube of its mean distance from the Sun".

T² ∝ r³

  • Mercury nearest to Sun: 88 days revolution.
  • Neptune farthest to Sun: 165 yrs revolution.

Mass Vs Weight

MassWeight
The mass of a body is the amount of matter present in itThe weight of a body is the force with which the earth attracts it
It has magnitude but not direction (scalar quantity)It has both magnitude and direction (vector quantity)
It does not change from place to placeIt changes from place to place (W = m × g)
It can never be zeroIt is zero at the center of earth
Its S.I. Unit is kilogramIts S.I. Unit is Newton

Variation in the gravity

  1. 1. The gravity is more at the poles than at the equator.
  2. 2. The gravity decreases with altitude.
  3. 3. The gravity on the moon is 1/6th of Earth's gravity.

F = GMm/R²

m × g = GMm/R²

g = GM/R²

g = 9.8 m/s²

  • M = Mass of the Earth
  • R = Radius of the Earth
  • G = Universal Gravitational Constant
  • g = Acceleration due to gravity

"g" represents the acceleration that an object experiences due to the Earth's gravity (or the gravity of any celestial body).

  • Gravity gets weaker as you move farther from Earth's center. This is because gravity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the centers of two objects.
  • When we go higher, the distance increases → gravity decreases.
  • As we move deeper into the Earth, only the Earth's mass beneath us contributes to the gravitational pull. The mass above us has no effect → gravity also decreases.
  • So, gravity is strongest at the surface and weaker both above and below it.

Thrust

  • Thrust is a force, or push, that acts on a surface in a direction perpendicular (normal) to that surface. It is measured in Newtons (N). E.g. Thrust is generated by the engines of the aircraft through some kind of propulsion system.

Pressure

  • Pressure is the force (or thrust) acting per unit area. S.I. unit is pascal (Pa).

Pressure = Thrust/Force / Area

P = Kg m / s² m² Or 1 Pa = N/m²

Pascal's Law

  • Pascal's law (also Pascal's principle or the principle of transmission of fluid-pressure) is a principle given by Blaise Pascal that states that "A pressure change at any point in a confined incompressible fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid such that the same change occurs everywhere".
  • It was given in 1653 and published in 1663.
  • 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa
  • 1 atm = 1.01325 bar
  • 1 N = 10⁵ Dyne

Gravitation and Work Done (continued)

Pascal's Principle (continued)

  • P₁ = F₁/A₁, P₂ = F₂/A₂
  • Pascal's principle: P₁ = P₂

Hydraulic press: Second force is 10 times original force. F₂ = P₂A₂ = 10 × F₁

Archimedes' Principle

  • Archimedes' principle states that "The upward buoyant force that is exerted on a body immersed in a fluid whether fully or partially is equal to the weight of the fluid that the body displaces".

F_b = ρgV

  • F_b = Buoyant force
  • ρ = Fluid density
  • g = Acceleration due to gravity
  • V = Fluid volume

E.g. A ship will float higher in saltwater than in freshwater because the denser saltwater exerts a greater buoyant force, requiring the ship to displace less volume of water to remain afloat. The same principle applies to a person swimming, who will feel lighter and easier to float in saltwater.

Bernoulli's Principle

  • Bernoulli's principle is a key concept in fluid dynamics. It states that "In a streamlined flow of incompressible, non-viscous fluid, the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy per unit volume remains constant".

Pressure energy + Kinetic energy + Potential energy = Constant

Relative Density

  • Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance (usually water for liquids and solids).

Relative Density = Density of a Substance / Density of Water

  • Density = Mass / Volume
  • S.I. unit of density is Kg/m³.
  • Relative Density has no S.I. unit.

Work and Energy

#### Work

  • "Work" is defined as the energy transferred by a force that causes an object to move a certain distance in the direction of the force. The S.I. unit is joule (J) which is equivalent to Newton-meter (Nm).

Work Done = Force × Displacement

Work Done = FS cos θ

  • Work done is a scalar quantity.
  • The S.I. unit of energy is joule. It is named after English physicist James Prescott Joule.
  • Work done is positive when force and displacement have same direction (are parallel to each other).
  • Work done is negative when force and displacement are in opposite directions (anti-parallel, angle 180°).
  • Work done is zero, when force and displacement are perpendicular (angle = 90°). Work done is zero when there is no displacement.
  • Positive Work: Force and displacement in same direction
  • Negative Work: Force and displacement in opposite directions
  • Zero Work: Force perpendicular to displacement

Gravitation and Work Done (continued)

Energy

  • Energy is defined as the capacity to do work, or the ability to cause change. It may exist in potential, kinetic, thermal, electrical, chemical, nuclear, or other various forms.
  • S.I. unit of energy is Joule (J). Biggest source of energy is the Sun.

Forms of Energy

#### Kinetic Energy

  • Kinetic energy refers to the energy possessed by an object due to its motion.

K.E. = ½ mV²

  • m = Mass
  • V = Velocity

Relationship between K.E. and Linear Momentum (p)

K.E. = ½ mV² × m/m = (mV)² / 2m = p² / 2m

p = mV

When Momentum is Doubled: If momentum (p) doubles, the kinetic energy (K.E.) becomes 4 times.

K.E. = (2p)² / 2m = 4p² / 2m

#### Potential Energy

  • Potential energy (P.E.) is stored energy that an object has because of its position or state, ready to be released and do work. E.g. Gravitational P.E.
  • The concept of a dam is fundamentally based on potential energy (P.E.), where the stored water at a height possesses potential energy that can be converted into kinetic energy (motion) and used in turbines to generate electricity or for other purposes.

P.E. = mgh

  • m = Mass of the body
  • g = Acceleration due to gravity
  • h = Height
  • P.E. (maximum), K.E. = 0
  • P.E. = K.E. (when at center point)
  • K.E. is maximum (just before touching the surface)

#### Escape Velocity

  • The velocity needed for a body to escape from a gravitational centre of attraction without undergoing any further acceleration. E.g. Imagine throwing a ball upwards, if you throw it lightly, it comes back down due to gravity; however, if you throw it with a high enough velocity, it will escape Earth's gravity and never return.
  • Escape velocity is approx. 11.2 km/s.

#### Law of Conservation

  • The law of conservation of energy states that "Energy can neither be created nor be destroyed. Although, it may be transformed from one form to another".
  • The 1st Law of Thermodynamics is based on this concept.

#### Energy Conversions (common examples)

  1. 1. Dynamo: It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  2. 2. Generator: It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  3. 3. Motor: It converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
  4. 4. Microphone: It converts sound energy into electrical energy.
  5. 5. Loudspeaker: It converts electrical energy into sound energy.
  6. 6. Photosynthesis: Process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy (primarily from sunlight) into chemical energy in the form of sugars, using carbon dioxide and water, and releasing oxygen as a byproduct.
  7. 7. Battery: It converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
  8. 8. Bulb: It converts electrical energy primarily into light energy and heat energy. Bulb filament is made of Tungsten (W).

Mechanical energy is defined as the total amount of potential energy (P.E.) and kinetic energy (K.E.) an object possesses.

Laws of Thermodynamics

#### Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics

  • It states that "If body A in thermal equilibrium with B, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A is also in thermal equilibrium with C".

#### First Law of Thermodynamics

  • It states that "Energy can neither be created nor be destroyed only converted from one form to another".
  • It is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat.

Formula: Q = ΔU + W

  • Q = Heat added to the system
  • ΔU = Change in internal energy
  • W = Work done by the system

Zeroth law was given by Ralph H. Fowler in 1931.

#### Second Law of Thermodynamics

  • Heat cannot flow from a colder body to a hotter body on its own.
  • It introduces the concept of entropy (disorder).

E.g. Heat engine can't be 100% efficient, refrigerator requires external work to transfer heat from cold to hot.

#### Third Law of Thermodynamics

  • As temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K), the entropy of a perfect crystal becomes zero.

Entropy, the measure of a system's thermal energy per unit temperature that is unavailable for doing useful work.

Power

  • Power is the rate at which work is done or the rate at which energy is transferred from one place to another or transformed from one type to another. The S.I. unit of power is Watt (W).

Gravitation and Work Done (continued)

Power (continued)

Power = Work / Time

Power = Force × Velocity

P = FV

A watt (W) is a unit of power, specifically defined as one joule of energy transferred or converted per second (1 J/s).

Horse Power

  • Horsepower (hp) is a unit of measurement of power, or the rate at which work is done, often used to describe the output of engines or motors.
  • 1 hp = 746 W
  • 1 hp = 0.746 kW
  • 1 kW = 1000 W
